candidates.bio: While the book of Proverbs [declares](https://www.sefaria.org/Proverbs.31.30?lang=en) that "beauty is vain" and only "fear of God" is praiseworthy, the Torah notes the beauty of many of its central characters – like Sarah, Rachel, and Joseph, to name a few. Biblical commentators, rabbinic literature, and works of musar and Jewish thought all reckon with the role beauty – physical beauty, spiritual beauty, the beauty of human and animal forms, beauty of the Temple, and more – plays in Judaism, analyzing when it is to be seen as a value to strive for and when it is to be dismissed as a frivolous distraction from more important matters.

Joseph was the patriarch Jacob's eleventh son and the first from his mother, Rachel. After being sold into Egypt as a slave by his brothers, he became a master dream interpreter and adviser to Pharaoh. Thanks to Joseph, his father, his brothers, and their families were all able to move to Egypt to escape the famine in Canaan.

The story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife, in the book of Genesis, recounts a challenging encounter for Joseph. The story lends itself to further interpretation, and texts from various genres have contributed different motivations for both Joseph and Potiphar's wife.

Joseph Karo, expelled from Spain as a child, was a rabbi, talmudist, mystic, and preemiment halakhic codifier. His best-known work, the Shulchan Arukh, was accepted in his lifetime and formally recognized thereafter as the definitive statement of Jewish legal and religious practice. He also wrote basic commentaries on Rambam's Mishneh Torah and Jacob ben Ashe's Arba'ah Turim, both of which were major sources for his own Shulchan Arukh. As a mystic, he also received heavenly revelations. Some of these were set down in writing and contributed to his decision to migrate to the land of Israel. There, he lived in Safed, where he supported the effort of his teacher, Rabbi Yaakov Berav, to revive traditional rabbinic ordination (Hebrew: semikhah).

R. Yose b. Chalafta learned from many teachers but was a disciple of R. Akiva. Preserving many traditions from his father, he served as an authority in transmitting them to his younger contemporaries. He is credited with the compilation of Seder Olam, the classical compendium of traditional history.
R. Yose b. Kippar was a student of R. Elazar b. Shamu'a and was an emissary from the Land of Israel to the ascendant Jewish community in Babylonia.
A moderate scholar who lived during the Hadrianic persecutions, R Yose b. Kisma advocated accomodation with the Romans.
R. Yose b. Yehudah was the son of the famed R. Yehudah b. Il'ai, as well as his student. He was often involved in disputes with R. Yehudah haNasi, as well as with scholars of his father's generation.

Petras. He was known by the epithet "ben Ari" (son of a lion) in honor of his father, as cited in tractate Yoma, where Zeira b. Hama addressed him with this title while recounting his father's remarkable deeds.

candidates.bio: Rabbi Yosef HaKohen was a Tanna, sage, and priest in the time of the Second Temple. He is cited in rabbinic literature, and several laws of priesthood, ritual purity, and mourning are derived from his name and deeds.

Rabbi Yosei b. Dormaskit was a Tanna of the third generation of Mishnaic sages. A student of Rabbi Eliezer b. Hyrcanus and a disputant of Rabbi Yehuda, he appears in the Talmud solely as an aggadist. His only halakhic statement, addressing whether the prohibition of orlah applies outside the Land of Israel, is transmitted in the name of his teacher Rabbi Eliezer the Great.

Rabbi Yosei b. Kisma was a Tanna of the third generation. The Gemara records a sharp dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei in a Tiberias synagogue that tore a Torah scroll; Rabbi Yosei b. Kisma predicted the synagogue would become a house of idolatry, which later occurred. His views on Roman decrees were more moderate than those of other sages. He disputed with Rabbi Hanina b. Teradion over public Torah study under Roman ban, and before dying asked to be buried deep to prevent grave desecration. Roman dignitaries attended his burial; upon returning they found Rabbi Hanina b. Teradion teaching Torah publicly and executed him by fire. The Gemara cites his teaching that the Son of David will come after a certain gate falls and is rebuilt repeatedly. He is traditionally buried on Mount

Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Yehuda was a Tanna of the final generation of Tannaim. The son of Rabbi Yehuda—one of the most frequently cited Tannaim in the Mishnah—and the grandson of Rabbi Elai, he lived in the generation of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He learned most of his Torah from his father, though the Talmud records him arguing with Rabbi Yehuda in halakhic discussions. He frequently disputes the older generation, including his father's colleagues and students of Rabbi Akiva such as Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, as well as his contemporary Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rabbi Yosei b. Shaul was a first-generation Eretz Yisraeli Amora.

candidates.bio: Rabbi Yosei b. Zimra was a Tanna and a priest who lived during the transitional period between the Tannaim and the Amoraim.

Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida was a fourth-generation Eretz Yisrael Amora. He appears frequently in both Talmuds in disputes with his colleague Rabbi Yona, and in the Jerusalem Talmud he is sometimes called Rabbi Yasa. A student of Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Zeira, he taught first in Rabbi Ila's yeshiva and later in his own, and was one of the closers of the sugyot in tractate Nezikin in the Jerusalem Talmud. He lived in Tiberias; when decrees increased in Eretz Yisrael he briefly descended to Babylonia with Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Bun, then returned to become the leading sage of his generation. All fifth-generation Eretz Yisrael Amoraim were his students, foremost among them Rabbi Mana, and his son was Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Yosei.

Rabbi Yosei ben ha-Chotef Efrati was an Eretz Yisraeli tanna of the fourth generation, mentioned once in the Mishnah in tractate Kilayim. The Jerusalem Talmud records that he studied under Rabbi Yishmael at the end of Rabbi Yishmael's life. His father's epithet ha-Chotef ("the snatcher") is explained in a responsum of Rabbi Menachem Azariah of Fano as denoting one who eagerly seized mitzvot in the marketplace; others speculate it referred to a particular incident or to hasty speech. The Jerusalem Talmud also cites a "Yosef Efrati" who served Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, apparently the same figure.

Rabbi Yosei beRabbi Bun (called Rabbi Yosei b. Avin in the Babylonian Talmud) was a fourth-generation Eretz Yisraeli Amora of the late fourth century CE. He appears primarily in the Jerusalem Talmud, where he is among the most frequently cited Amoraim, and only rarely in the Babylonian Talmud. He was a student of Rabbi Yosei of Yokrat, and according to Aharon Heiman his father was the Amora Rabbi Avin. In the Jerusalem Talmud he often debates halakha with Rabbi Mana and his students, and his statements typically conclude the sugya. He emended or explained traditions from Rabbi Yochanan and brought Babylonian traditions. Rabbi Yosei ha-Glila was an Eretz Yisrael Amora of the third–fourth generation. He was likely a student of Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina and a colleague of Rabbi Yonah. The Babylonian Talmud recounts that he once carried a lamp on Shabbat in the presence of Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, relying on the view of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina objected to this.

Rabbi Yosei ha-Kohen was a second-generation Tanna of the late first century CE and a student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. The Mishnah calls him a hasid, a title his teacher and peers used; some identify him with Rabbi Yosei Ketanta. His halachic statements appear only once in the Mishnah, an absence attributed to hasidic humility. The Babylonian Talmud records that he studied Ma'aseh Merkavah with Rabbi Yehoshua and that Rabban Yochanan praised his knowledge of hidden wisdom. It also notes that his handwriting was never held by a non-Jew due to Sabbath caution. He appears in aggadic contexts interpreting verses before Rabban Gamliel, answering his teacher's ethical questions about neighbors, and comforting Rabban Yochanan upon the death of his son. Rabbi Yosei of Yokrat was a third-generation Amora and teacher of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin. His hometown, Yokrat, is unidentified today. The Talmud recounts three stories about him: two depict extreme piety bordering on harshness toward his children—he cursed his son for ripening figs out of season, and told his beautiful daughter to "return to dust" so men would not sin, prompting his student Rabbi Yosei bar Avin to leave him for Rav Ashi; the third describes a donkey he rented out returning home with its wages. Some modern scholars argue he is not a historical figure, suggesting the tales symbolize the decline of the Eretz Yisrael center.

Rabbi Yosei Tzidonia was an Eretz Yisrael Amora of the fourth generation. He was called Tzidonia because he lived in Tzidon or Tel Beit Tzaida. He was a student of Rabbi Yirmeya and reviewed baraitot before him. He transmitted oral teachings in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

Rav Yosef b. Abba was a Babylonian Amora who studied under Rabbi Yochanan, Shmuel, and Rav Yehuda. He is mentioned several times in the Talmud, including in a discussion on validating documents in the absence of a litigant, where he explains Rabbi Yochanan’s reasoning by deriving from the verse “and it be testified to its owner” that no legal judgment may be validated without the litigant’s presence. He was a contemporary of Rabba bar Yirmeya, and the Talmud records a joint discussion they held when Rabba bar Yirmeya came to his city.

Rav Yosef b. Ami was a Babylonian Amora of the fifth generation. He is mentioned only twice in the Talmud, in one instance raising a contradiction between two statements of Rava. The author of Erech Tannaim veAmoraim infers from this that he belonged to the later generations, and hypothesizes that he may have been the brother of Rav Pinchas b. Ami; if so, he lived in the time of Rav Ashi.

A contemporary of Rabbah, Rav Yosef became the head of the academy in Pumpedita after Rabbah's death. He was known for his humility and for his mastery of the corpus of Jewish law. While wealthy, Rav Yosef had health issues which brought him blindness and the loss of memory.

Rav Yosef b. Hama was a Babylonian Amora of the third generation who lived in Mechoza. He was a student of Rav Sheshet, though some of his statements in the Talmud are also cited in the name of Rav Nachman bar Yaakov. His son was Rava, a leading Amora and head of the Pumbedita Yeshiva in Mechoza.

Rav Yosef b. Rava was a seventh-generation Babylonian Amora, the son of Rava, and head of the Pumbedita yeshiva. He studied under Rav Yosef for six years. It is related that after his engagement he went to study with Rav Yosef; when he returned home early to see his wife, his father Rava came out toward him with weapons, enraged that he remembered his wife instead of being immersed in Torah, and their quarrel caused them both to miss the pre-Yom Kippur meal. His father helped him understand difficult teachings of Rav Yosef, such as reconciling conflicting opinions on how many incidents establish a chazakah. He reported his father's stringencies, including never walking without tzitzit, and assisted Rava in complex rulings, notably technical examinations in the laws of treifot.

R. Yose b. Abun (or Avin or Bun) is one of the names that appears most frequently in the Yerushalmi. He is from the last group of scholars mentioned there by name and is thought to have had a major role in the Yerushalmi's formation. He often cites earlier traditions from Babylonia as well as from the Land of Israel and seeks to clarify them.

candidates.bio: While the book of Proverbs [declares](https://www.sefaria.org/Proverbs.31.30?lang=en) that "beauty is vain" and only "fear of God" is praiseworthy, the Torah notes the beauty of many of its central characters – like Sarah, Rachel, and Joseph, to name a few. Biblical commentators, rabbinic literature, and works of musar and Jewish thought all reckon with the role beauty – physical beauty, spiritual beauty, the beauty of human and animal forms, beauty of the Temple, and more – plays in Judaism, analyzing when it is to be seen as a value to strive for and when it is to be dismissed as a frivolous distraction from more important matters.

Joseph was the patriarch Jacob's eleventh son and the first from his mother, Rachel. After being sold into Egypt as a slave by his brothers, he became a master dream interpreter and adviser to Pharaoh. Thanks to Joseph, his father, his brothers, and their families were all able to move to Egypt to escape the famine in Canaan.

The story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife, in the book of Genesis, recounts a challenging encounter for Joseph. The story lends itself to further interpretation, and texts from various genres have contributed different motivations for both Joseph and Potiphar's wife.

Joseph Karo, expelled from Spain as a child, was a rabbi, talmudist, mystic, and preemiment halakhic codifier. His best-known work, the Shulchan Arukh, was accepted in his lifetime and formally recognized thereafter as the definitive statement of Jewish legal and religious practice. He also wrote basic commentaries on Rambam's Mishneh Torah and Jacob ben Ashe's Arba'ah Turim, both of which were major sources for his own Shulchan Arukh. As a mystic, he also received heavenly revelations. Some of these were set down in writing and contributed to his decision to migrate to the land of Israel. There, he lived in Safed, where he supported the effort of his teacher, Rabbi Yaakov Berav, to revive traditional rabbinic ordination (Hebrew: semikhah).

R. Yose b. Chalafta learned from many teachers but was a disciple of R. Akiva. Preserving many traditions from his father, he served as an authority in transmitting them to his younger contemporaries. He is credited with the compilation of Seder Olam, the classical compendium of traditional history.
R. Yose b. Kippar was a student of R. Elazar b. Shamu'a and was an emissary from the Land of Israel to the ascendant Jewish community in Babylonia.
A moderate scholar who lived during the Hadrianic persecutions, R Yose b. Kisma advocated accomodation with the Romans.
R. Yose b. Yehudah was the son of the famed R. Yehudah b. Il'ai, as well as his student. He was often involved in disputes with R. Yehudah haNasi, as well as with scholars of his father's generation.

candidates.bio: Rabbi Yosef HaKohen was a Tanna, sage, and priest in the time of the Second Temple. He is cited in rabbinic literature, and several laws of priesthood, ritual purity, and mourning are derived from his name and deeds.

Rabbi Yosei b. Dormaskit was a Tanna of the third generation of Mishnaic sages. A student of Rabbi Eliezer b. Hyrcanus and a disputant of Rabbi Yehuda, he appears in the Talmud solely as an aggadist. His only halakhic statement, addressing whether the prohibition of orlah applies outside the Land of Israel, is transmitted in the name of his teacher Rabbi Eliezer the Great.

Rabbi Yosei b. Kisma was a Tanna of the third generation. The Gemara records a sharp dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei in a Tiberias synagogue that tore a Torah scroll; Rabbi Yosei b. Kisma predicted the synagogue would become a house of idolatry, which later occurred. His views on Roman decrees were more moderate than those of other sages. He disputed with Rabbi Hanina b. Teradion over public Torah study under Roman ban, and before dying asked to be buried deep to prevent grave desecration. Roman dignitaries attended his burial; upon returning they found Rabbi Hanina b. Teradion teaching Torah publicly and executed him by fire. The Gemara cites his teaching that the Son of David will come after a certain gate falls and is rebuilt repeatedly. He is traditionally buried on Mount

Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Yehuda was a Tanna of the final generation of Tannaim. The son of Rabbi Yehuda—one of the most frequently cited Tannaim in the Mishnah—and the grandson of Rabbi Elai, he lived in the generation of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He learned most of his Torah from his father, though the Talmud records him arguing with Rabbi Yehuda in halakhic discussions. He frequently disputes the older generation, including his father's colleagues and students of Rabbi Akiva such as Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, as well as his contemporary Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rabbi Yosei b. Shaul was a first-generation Eretz Yisraeli Amora.

candidates.bio: Rabbi Yosei b. Zimra was a Tanna and a priest who lived during the transitional period between the Tannaim and the Amoraim.

Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida was a fourth-generation Eretz Yisrael Amora. He appears frequently in both Talmuds in disputes with his colleague Rabbi Yona, and in the Jerusalem Talmud he is sometimes called Rabbi Yasa. A student of Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Zeira, he taught first in Rabbi Ila's yeshiva and later in his own, and was one of the closers of the sugyot in tractate Nezikin in the Jerusalem Talmud. He lived in Tiberias; when decrees increased in Eretz Yisrael he briefly descended to Babylonia with Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Bun, then returned to become the leading sage of his generation. All fifth-generation Eretz Yisrael Amoraim were his students, foremost among them Rabbi Mana, and his son was Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Yosei.

Rabbi Yosei ben ha-Chotef Efrati was an Eretz Yisraeli tanna of the fourth generation, mentioned once in the Mishnah in tractate Kilayim. The Jerusalem Talmud records that he studied under Rabbi Yishmael at the end of Rabbi Yishmael's life. His father's epithet ha-Chotef ("the snatcher") is explained in a responsum of Rabbi Menachem Azariah of Fano as denoting one who eagerly seized mitzvot in the marketplace; others speculate it referred to a particular incident or to hasty speech. The Jerusalem Talmud also cites a "Yosef Efrati" who served Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, apparently the same figure.

Rabbi Yosei beRabbi Bun (called Rabbi Yosei b. Avin in the Babylonian Talmud) was a fourth-generation Eretz Yisraeli Amora of the late fourth century CE. He appears primarily in the Jerusalem Talmud, where he is among the most frequently cited Amoraim, and only rarely in the Babylonian Talmud. He was a student of Rabbi Yosei of Yokrat, and according to Aharon Heiman his father was the Amora Rabbi Avin. In the Jerusalem Talmud he often debates halakha with Rabbi Mana and his students, and his statements typically conclude the sugya. He emended or explained traditions from Rabbi Yochanan and brought Babylonian traditions. He is traditionally credited with editing the Jerusalem Talmud, paralleling Rav Ashi's editing of the Babylonian Talmud. Later Eretz Yisraeli Amoraim are not mentioned by n

Rabbi Yosei ha-Glila was an Eretz Yisrael Amora of the third–fourth generation. He was likely a student of Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina and a colleague of Rabbi Yonah. The Babylonian Talmud recounts that he once carried a lamp on Shabbat in the presence of Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, relying on the view of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina objected to this.

Rabbi Yosei ha-Kohen was a second-generation Tanna of the late first century CE and a student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. The Mishnah calls him a hasid, a title his teacher and peers used; some identify him with Rabbi Yosei Ketanta. His halachic statements appear only once in the Mishnah, an absence attributed to hasidic humility. The Babylonian Talmud records that he studied Ma'aseh Merkavah with Rabbi Yehoshua and that Rabban Yochanan praised his knowledge of hidden wisdom. It also notes that his handwriting was never held by a non-Jew due to Sabbath caution. He appears in aggadic contexts interpreting verses before Rabban Gamliel, answering his teacher's ethical questions about neighbors, and comforting Rabban Yochanan upon the death of his son. Rabbi Yosei of Yokrat was a third-generation Amora and teacher of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin. His hometown, Yokrat, is unidentified today. The Talmud recounts three stories about him: two depict extreme piety bordering on harshness toward his children—he cursed his son for ripening figs out of season, and told his beautiful daughter to "return to dust" so men would not sin, prompting his student Rabbi Yosei bar Avin to leave him for Rav Ashi; the third describes a donkey he rented out returning home with its wages. Some modern scholars argue he is not a historical figure, suggesting the tales symbolize the decline of the Eretz Yisrael center.

Rabbi Yosei Tzidonia was an Eretz Yisrael Amora of the fourth generation. He was called Tzidonia because he lived in Tzidon or Tel Beit Tzaida. He was a student of Rabbi Yirmeya and reviewed baraitot before him. He transmitted oral teachings in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

Rav Yosef b. Abba was a Babylonian Amora who studied under Rabbi Yochanan, Shmuel, and Rav Yehuda. He is mentioned several times in the Talmud, including in a discussion on validating documents in the absence of a litigant, where he explains Rabbi Yochanan’s reasoning by deriving from the verse “and it be testified to its owner” that no legal judgment may be validated without the litigant’s presence. He was a contemporary of Rabba bar Yirmeya, and the Talmud records a joint discussion they held when Rabba bar Yirmeya came to his city.

Rav Yosef b. Ami was a Babylonian Amora of the fifth generation. He is mentioned only twice in the Talmud, in one instance raising a contradiction between two statements of Rava. The author of Erech Tannaim veAmoraim infers from this that he belonged to the later generations, and hypothesizes that he may have been the brother of Rav Pinchas b. Ami; if so, he lived in the time of Rav Ashi.

A contemporary of Rabbah, Rav Yosef became the head of the academy in Pumpedita after Rabbah's death. He was known for his humility and for his mastery of the corpus of Jewish law. While wealthy, Rav Yosef had health issues which brought him blindness and the loss of memory.

Rav Yosef b. Hama was a Babylonian Amora of the third generation who lived in Mechoza. He was a student of Rav Sheshet, though some of his statements in the Talmud are also cited in the name of Rav Nachman bar Yaakov. His son was Rava, a leading Amora and head of the Pumbedita Yeshiva in Mechoza.

Rav Yosef b. Rava was a seventh-generation Babylonian Amora, the son of Rava, and head of the Pumbedita yeshiva. He studied under Rav Yosef for six years. It is related that after his engagement he went to study with Rav Yosef; when he returned home early to see his wife, his father Rava came out toward him with weapons, enraged that he remembered his wife instead of being immersed in Torah, and their quarrel caused them both to miss the pre-Yom Kippur meal. His father helped him understand difficult teachings of Rav Yosef, such as reconciling conflicting opinions on how many incidents establish a chazakah. He reported his father's stringencies, including never walking without tzitzit, and assisted Rava in complex rulings, notably technical examinations in the laws of treifot.

R. Yose b. Abun (or Avin or Bun) is one of the names that appears most frequently in the Yerushalmi. He is from the last group of scholars mentioned there by name and is thought to have had a major role in the Yerushalmi's formation. He often cites earlier traditions from Babylonia as well as from the Land of Israel and seeks to clarify them.

data.reason: On the quail verse, the passage reads: 'Rabbi Yosi says: He let them fall by the camp, a day's journey this way... three parasangs to each side'. 'Others say' follows. Just before (in the saved context), Rabbi Meir gives his own reading of the same words. Later the passage names 'Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yose HaGelili'. Reader-c held: the name is bare, and 'tannaitic' is a fact about the work, not the words. Reader-d accepted on the dispute form and the passage's separate use of the HaGelili epithet. The text writes 'HaGelili' when it means that Yose. So the plain form is a different person, and the caution keeps them apart. The plain Yosi gives an opinion in a row with Rabbi Meir and 'others'. That is a dispute among tannaim on one verse. An amora would not appear in that form in this work. The registry's only tanna named plainly Rabbi Yose is rabbi-yose-b-chalafta. All other tannaitic Yose entries carry a father or epithet. Adjudication-01 captured a public reference: 'an unqualified Rabbi Yosi mentioned in the Mishnah is Rabbi Yosi ben Chalafta'. It speaks of the Mishnah, not this midrash, so it supports the convention only by extension. No parallel outside Sifrei Zuta exists in the saved corpus. Accept rabbi-yose-b-chalafta, on the same basis adjudication-01 used for case-064359ce301beac5ae4b, with that gap stated.

source.before: יח חלב של שור הנסקל שאין חייבין עליו משום בל תותר. אמרו לו אשם תלוי כדבריך יוכיח שחייבין עליו משום בל תותר ואין טעון שריפה התורה אמרה תשביתו שאר מבתיכם משביתו אתה בכל דבר: כי כל אוכל חמץ. מכלל שנאמר (י"ב י"ט) כי כל אוכל מחמצת אין לי אלא שנתחמץ מאליו שנתחמץ מידי אחרים מניין ת"ל כי כל אכל חמץ: ונכרתה הנפש. ולא הצבור: ההוא. לא אנוס ולא שוגג ולא מוטעה: מישראל. וישראל בשלום: מיום הראשון עד יום השביעי. יכול אין יום הראשון ויום השביעי בכלל כשם שנאמר במצורע (ויקרא י"ג י"ב) מראשו ועד רגליו ואין הראש והרגלים בכלל ת"ל (י"ב י"ח) עד יום האחד ועשרים לחדש בערב. רבי אומר מקומו מוכרע מיום הראשון עד יום השביעי.

source.before: יח חלב של שור הנסקל שאין חייבין עליו משום בל תותר. אמרו לו אשם תלוי כדבריך יוכיח שחייבין עליו משום בל תותר ואין טעון שריפה התורה אמרה תשביתו שאר מבתיכם משביתו אתה בכל דבר: כי כל אוכל חמץ. מכלל שנאמר (י"ב י"ט) כי כל אוכל מחמצת אין לי אלא שנתחמץ מאליו שנתחמץ מידי אחרים מניין ת"ל כי כל אכל חמץ: ונכרתה הנפש. ולא הצבור: ההוא. לא אנוס ולא שוגג ולא מוטעה: מישראל. וישראל בשלום: מיום הראשון עד יום השביעי. יכול אין יום הראשון ויום השביעי בכלל כשם שנאמר במצורע (ויקרא י"ג י"ב) מראשו ועד רגליו ואין הראש והרגלים בכלל ת"ל (י"ב י"ח) עד יום האחד ועשרים לחדש בערב. רבי אומר מקומו מוכרע מיום הראשון עד יום השביעי.
source.passage: וביום הראשון מקרא קודש קדשהו, במה אתה מקדשו קדשהו במאכל קדשהו במשתה וקדשהו בכסות נקייה: ביום הראשון מקרא קדש וביום השביעי מקרא קדש. אין לי אלא יום טוב ראשון ואחרון שאסורין במלאכה חולו של מועד מניין, אמרת ומה יום טוב ראשון ואחרון שאין לפניהם ואחריהם מקודשין אסורין במלאכה חולו של מועד שלפניהם ואחריהם מקודשין אינו דין שיהו אסורין במלאכה: הרי ששת ימי בראשית יוכיחו שלפניהם ואחריהם מקודשין ואין אסורין במלאכה: לא אם אמרת בששת ימי בראשית שאין עמהן קרבן מוסף תאמר בחולו של מועד שיש עמהן קרבן מוסף: הרי ראשי חדשים יוכיחו שיש עמהן קרבן מוסף ואין אסורין במלאכה: לא אם אמרת בראשי חדשים שאין קרויין מקרא קדש תאמר באלו שקרויין מקרא קודש הואיל וקרויין מקרא קדש דין הוא שיהוא אסורין במלאכה: כל מלאכה לא יעשה בהם. יכול לא יקנב את הירק ולא ידיח את הכלים ולא יציע את המטות הרי אתה דן נאמר כאן מלאכה ונאמר מלאכה במשכן מה מלאכה האמורה במשכן מלאכה שיש עמה מחשבה אף מלאכה האמורה כאן מלאכה שיש עמה מחשבה, או מה מלאכה האמורה במשכן מלאכה גמורה אף כאן אין לי אלא מלאכה גמורה שלא יכתוב כל הספר ושלא יארוג את כל הבגד ושלא יעשה את כל הנפה, מניין שלא יכתוב שתי אותיות ולא יארוג שני חוטין ולא יעשה שני בתי נירין בסלין ובסוגין בנפה ובכברה ת"ל מלאכה כל מלאכה, אין לי אלא ברשות במצוה מניין לא יכתוב שתי אותיות בספרים בתפילין ובמזוזות לא יארוג שני חוטין בכתנת ובמכנסים ובמעיל ת"ל מלאכה כל מלאכה, אין לי אלא מלאכה שחייבין עליה חטאת מלאכה שאין חייבין עליה חטאת מניין לא יכתוב אות אחת ולא יארוג חוט אחד ולא יעשה בית אחד בסלין ובסוגין בנפה ובכברה [ת"ל] מלאכה כל מלאכה: אין לי אלא ברשות במצוה מניין לא יכתוב אות אחת בספרים בתפלין ובמזוזות ולא יארוג חוט אחד בכתנת ובמכנסים ובמעיל ת"ל מלאכה כל מלאכה: אין לי אלא מלאכה שחייבין על מינה חטאת מלאכה שאין חייבין על מינה חטאת מניין לא עולין באילן ולא רוכבין על גבי בהמה ולא שטין על פני המים ולא מספקין ולא מטפחין ולא מרקדין ת"ל מלאכה כל מלאכה , אין לי אלא ברשות במצוה מניין אין מקדישין ואין מעריכין ואין מחרימין ואין מגביהין תרומות ומעשרות ת"ל (ויקרא כ"ד כ"ג) שבתון שבות: אילו אומר לא יעשה בהם אשר יאכל לכל נפש הייתי אומר את שהוא אוכל נפש לא יעשה בהם ואת שאינו אוכל נפש יעשה בהם ת"ל אך הפסיק הענין דברי ר' יוסי הגלילי: כיוצא בו אתה אומר (מלכים א' ח' ט') אין בארון רק שני לוחות אבנים יכול שלא היו בו שני לחות אבנים ת"ל רק הפסיק הענין דברי ר' יוסי הגלילי: כיוצא בו אתה אומר (מלכים א' כ"ב ט"ז) אשר לא תדבר אלי רק אמת בשם ה' יכול שאמר לו אל תדבר לי אמת ת"ל רק הפסיק הענין דברי ר' יוסי הגלילי: כיוצא בו אתה אומר (מלכים א' ט"ו ה') אשר עשה דוד הישר בעיני ה' ולא סר מכל אשר צוהו כל ימי חייו רק בדבר אוריה החתי יכול בדבר אוריה החתי לא סר אבל סר בדברי אחרים ת"ל רק הפסיק הענין דברי ר' יוסי הגלילי: כיוצא בו אתה אומר (יהושע י"א י"ב) לא נותר ענקים בארץ ישראל רק בעזה בגת ובאשדוד נשארו, יכול בעזה בגת ובאשדוד לא נותר אבל נותר בשאר מקומות ת"ל רק הפסיק הענין דברי ר' יוסי הגלילי: אמר לו ר' עקיבה ומה אני צריך והלא כבר נותרו אלא מלמד שנכנסה בהן מארה והיו מתמעטין והולכין: הוא לבדו. מה ת"ל לבדו מלמד שאין בוררין ואין טוחנין ואין מרקדין: ומניין לעושה מדורה ומתחמם כנגדה מחימין לו חמין ורוחץ בהן ידיו ורגליו ומרחיץ בהן תינוק ת"ל לכם לכל שצרככם: יכול יעשה מן היום למחר ת"ל אשר יאכל לכל נפש יעשה בהם את שנאכל בהם יעשה ואת שאין נאכל בהם לא יעשה, או אשר יאכל לכל נפש שומע אני אף נפשות בהמה שהיא קרויה נפש כענין שנאמר (ויקרא כ"ד י"ח) ומכה נפש בהמה ישלמנה יכול יהוא מהלקטין מורסן לתורנגלים ועושין לימודין לכלבים ת"ל לכם לכם ולא לגוים לכם ולא לכלבים: מעשה בשמעון התימני שלא בא בלילי יום טוב לבית המדרש, לשחרית מצאו ר' יהודה בן באבא אמר לו מפני מה לא באתה אמש לבית המדרש אמר לו מצוה אחת אירע לי ועשיתיה, בלשת נכנסו לעיר והיינו מתיראין שלא יצהיבו את בני העיר שחטנו להם עגל אחד והאכלנום והשקינום וסכנום שלא יצהיבו את בני העיר אמר לו תמיה אני אם לא יצא שברך בהפסידך שהרי אמרו אין עושין ביום טוב לא לאכילת גוים ולא לאכילת כלבים: לכם. לכם ולא לגבוה שהיה אבא שאול דנו דין אחר ומה אם בשעה שלא נפתחו בידי הדיוט נפתחו בידי שמים, בשעה שנפתחו בידי הדיוט דין הוא שיפתחו בידי שמים:
